headline: New Zealand Parliament Passes Planning Overhaul Amid Grocery and Transparency Disputes
summary: Parliament passed two major bills to replace the Resource Management Act, with the Government arguing they will speed up housing, infrastructure and production while opponents warned of weaker environmental protections, higher costs for councils and reduced Māori participation. The sitting also featured clashes over supermarket competition, household costs and allegations that education officials sought to keep curriculum discussions off the written record. MPs passed legislation for a three-day postnatal stay and faster approvals for agricultural products, while Treaty settlement bills advanced to select committee.

topicSummaries.topic: Supermarket Duopoly Faces Renewed Scrutiny Over Grocery Prices
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Food prices affect household budgets, and the debate focused on whether Government measures will deliver meaningful competition and lower grocery costs.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Arena Williams pressed Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer on the concentration of the grocery market, which she said is dominated by two chains with 80 percent market share, and asked why the Government had not acted on advice to pursue structural changes. Brewer cited easier supermarket consents, stronger supplier protections and an independent cost-benefit analysis that identified restructuring Foodstuffs as an option for further testing. He said food-price inflation had slowed and that the Government would seek a mandate before asking the Commerce Commission to do further work. Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March advocated a publicly owned competitor; Brewer rejected the proposal, while the exchange underscored disagreement over whether market-led measures are sufficient.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Where is the third entrant that Nicola Willis said she wanted to get on and work with to get them in the door, who she would do a deal with to give them the VIP treatment?

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Brewer (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This Government will seek a mandate and then we will unleash the Commerce Commission to do the necessary work. If there are benefits for the New Zealand consumer, then we will proceed.

topicSummaries.topic: MPs Pass Resource Management Replacement Bills 67–54
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The new planning and environmental framework will shape how housing, infrastructure, farming and resource use are approved, as well as how environmental and Māori interests are weighed.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill at third reading, each by 67 votes to 54, advancing the Government’s plan to repeal and replace the Resource Management Act. Ministers said the changes would standardise planning, reduce consenting requirements and strengthen property rights; ACT MP Simon Court said officials estimated about 45 percent of current consents and permit applications could be removed. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bills, raising concerns about environmental protections, climate effects, ministerial discretion, possible costs to ratepayers and changes to iwi participation. Critics also highlighted provisions barring decision-makers from considering adverse climate effects and a pause to the Waikato River plan change; the Government said the new system would include environmental limits and uphold Treaty settlement redress. Implementation details and national standards are still to come.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: For New Zealanders, here is what our new system looks like for them: fewer consents and fewer permits; fewer plans developed faster; long-term certainty to developers, council, and the Government; more consistency through standardisation; and a more proportionate system; and relief for impositions on property.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Brooking (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It’s the Minister, and that is no way to have a major, important regulatory system for this country.

topicSummaries.topic: Education OIA Dispute Triggers Urgent Debate and Review
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns whether public records will show how ministerial input shaped school curriculum decisions, a matter affecting public accountability and trust in government.
topicSummaries.content: Labour and Green MPs raised reports that a senior Ministry of Education official advised staff not to put exchanges with the Education Minister’s office about curriculum changes in writing, citing the Official Information Act. Labour’s Ginny Andersen alleged an effort to avoid transparency and called for an independent curriculum and assessment council. Education Minister Erica Stanford denied that she or her staff had directed anyone to evade the Act, and said the Secretary for Education had alerted the Public Service Commissioner and Ombudsman, launched an internal review and begun an employment process. The urgent debate ended without a decision by the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Now, this is a clear attempt to avoid transparency, and it is a clear attempt to hide the Minister’s involvement in determining the exact content of what our children learn in the school curriculum.

keyExchanges.speaker: Erica Stanford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I want to be very clear and put on the record in Hansard that not myself or anybody else in my office has ever directed or even suggested that anyone should not comply with the OIA, or do anything other than fully comply with it, or should not be subverting it in anyway.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Rejects Cost-of-Living Criticism as Opposition Cites Jobs and Prices
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchange covered employment, wages, taxes, rents and household bills—issues with direct consequences for workers, renters and families.
topicSummaries.content: Opposition Leader Chris Hipkins challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon over the cost of living, public-sector job reductions, tuition costs and whether wages would outpace inflation. Luxon rejected Hipkins’ characterisation and pointed to economic growth, falling food-price inflation and zero annual rent increases in the latest data cited by Finance Minister Nicola Willis. Labour also questioned how many pay-equity claims had been settled under the Government’s revised system. Luxon defended the Government’s tax settings and argued that households would be better off by keeping more of their income.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: When real wages have fallen; power prices have been going up; insurance prices have been going up; rates have been going up; and other household costs, like food, have been going up—all by more than 20 percent under his leadership in just the last two years—will he now admit that the cost of living crisis is not only not over, it’s been getting worse under his leadership?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I refute the characterisation in that question, but what I’d say to the member is that if he feels so strongly about rates increases, why doesn’t he come out and reverse his position again and vote for the rates cap.

topicSummaries.topic: Three-Day Postnatal Stay Entitlement Passes, with Full Rollout by 2029
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law gives mothers the option of up to three days of inpatient postnatal care, subject to a phased rollout intended to expand capacity and staffing.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament passed the Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) (3-Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill, establishing an entitlement for mothers to choose at least three days of inpatient postnatal care. The Government said Budget 2026 provides $34.4 million over four years for maternity capacity and workforce support, with first-time mothers prioritised initially and full delivery planned by 1 July 2029. Labour and Green MPs supported the bill but raised concerns about staffing, service capacity and the removal of a requirement for maternity carers to inform women of the entitlement. ACT supported the measure while questioning whether legislation was needed to guide decisions made by clinicians and families.

keyExchanges.speaker: Casey Costello (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This Government is backing this legislation with a significant financial uplift of $34.4 million over four years through Budget 2026.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: One of the changes to the bill in the course of its life has been the deferred start until 2029, the addition of an implementation plan, as I’ve mentioned.

topicSummaries.topic: Agricultural Product Approval Rules Reformed, Greens Oppose Bill
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Farmers and growers may gain faster access to overseas-approved medicines and crop treatments, while the debate raised questions about safeguards for people, animals and the environment.
topicSummaries.content: The Agricultural Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Amendment Bill passed its third reading by 101 votes to 21. It allows New Zealand regulators to rely more on assessments by trusted overseas regulators while still considering local risks; Food Safety Minister Andrew Hoggard said the change would reduce duplication without lowering standards. Labour supported the bill but cited concerns about its shortened process and safeguards, while the Greens opposed it, arguing that overseas assessments could weaken precaution around pesticides and herbicides. Ministers said the bill does not change the separate regulatory framework for genetically modified organisms under the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act.

keyExchanges.speaker: Andrew Hoggard (National)
keyExchanges.quote: So let me be very clear: we are not cutting corners, we are cutting duplication.

keyExchanges.speaker: Steve Abel (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: On balance, we do not believe that this amendment meets the right balance.

topicSummaries.topic: Ngāti Mutunga and Shared Moriori Redress Bills Advance
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bills set out steps toward redress for Crown breaches and establish shared arrangements for cultural sites and local planning on the Chatham Islands.
topicSummaries.content: The Ngāti Mutunga o Wharekauri Claims Settlement Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Māori Affairs Committee. In the extended sitting, the Rēkohu Wharekauri Shared Redress Bill also passed its first reading and went to the committee for scrutiny. The shared-redress proposal provides for shared management of Te Whanga Lagoon, a joint planning committee, cultural redress properties and restored traditional place names. The Government said Moriori had not signed the shared deed at the time of the debate; MPs noted that overlapping interests and concerns about tino rangatiratanga would require careful consideration as the bill proceeds.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill, before the House today, differs from many of the settlement bills that have come before it. It’s bespoke and unique in nature.

keyExchanges.speaker: Steve Abel (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Moriori have concerns around the settlement implications with Wharekauri and questions of tino rangatiratanga.

conclusion: The Government secured passage of its resource-management overhaul and several other bills, but disputes over household costs, environmental safeguards, Māori participation and government transparency remain unresolved.
